#4186. The Sims 4 developer hasn't forgotten about its quality of life commitment, and is back with an update on what to expect in 2026

Maxis has offered some fresh details on its long-running mission to improve player quality of life in The Sims 4.

As the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of new content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

The quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one update on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

In the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of issues should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

The first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

The infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo issues, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Another important area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

The good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next update will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported issues.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.

#4184. Pokémon GO Players Can Claim Free Pikachu Crocs Avatar Item

Scott Baird is a Contributor from the UK with over a decade of video game writing experience.

Halloween might be over, but Pokémon Go is giving the chance to unleash horrors upon its world, as the worst clothing item ever produced by human hands is coming to the game, and fans can acquire it for free.

It's quite refreshing to be able to make some actual progress in a mobile title without opening my wallet. Thanks, Pokemon GO.

Pokémon Go has had multiple controversies regarding player avatars; back when Niantic was running the game, there was a massive downgrade in character quality. Suddenly, characters lacked curves, and everyone became a generic outline, with detail plummeting across the board.

The backlash against the bad Pokémon Go avatars has diminished over time, but that hasn’t stopped the game from receiving some terrible outfits. The next one involves a type of shoe that is an abomination upon humanity, and one set of them is available in Pokémon Go for free.

Crocs are the worst shoes ever made, being marginally better than leather boots filled with thumb tacks worn by masochists. However, people buy them, and this has led to geek crossovers such as Yu-Gi-Oh! Crocs, and recently, Pokémon.

The official Pokémon Go website has announced that the Crocs crossover has arrived in the game and will run until December 31, 2027, giving players ample time to acquire them. One of the sets is completely free, being the Pokémon Pikachu Classic Clog item, which can be claimed by using the code POKÉMONGOxCROCSxELECTRIFYING in the game.

Pokemon Go's Scattered to the Winds event is bringing new Shiny forms and expanding the Gift limit for players.

Two other sets of Pokémon Go Crocs can be claimed: Pokémon Gengar Classic Clog and Pokémon Jigglypuff Classic Clog. These can only be claimed by the sickos who purchased them in real life, and they’ll be sent a free code to download them.

The player avatar in Pokémon Go is pretty small, and they don’t appear on the screen all that much, as the game is mostly focused on catching Pokémon and battles. That being said, players care about how their in-game avatar looks, often going for attractive, cool, or downright weird models to stand out from the crowd. This is why the in-game cosmetics industry is so profitable.

Niantic has revealed that one of the Pokemon Go March 2025 events is a Fuecoco-filled Community Day.

Pokémon Go has plenty of paid avatar items, some of which are tied to limited events. There are also lots of free avatar items, unlocked by completing tasks, giving players a reason to log in every day. All of them, without fail, are better-looking than the Pokémon Crocs collection.

Then again, there’s a certain kind of fan that loves the items everyone hates. Indeed, some people wear Crocs for this exact reason, imagining themselves as some kind of Cyberpunk-era James Dean rebel, wearing their awful plastic shoes with holes in them, rather than the sad, soulless wretches they truly are.

Perhaps the idea behind this crossover is to attract the Pokémon Go whales who buy everything associated with the game. They’ll have to buy some Gengar and Jigglypuff Crocs to stay in the loop and ensure they have every avatar item at their fingertips. Whether such fans remain after years of lackluster Pokémon Go updates remains to be seen.

In the end, it’s hard to be mad at a company giving away goodies for free. Maybe there’s a fan out there who is still stuck with the basic Pokémon Go avatar shoes and wants something a bit nicer for their little character to strut around the overworld in. Maybe that’s the point of all this, as walking around in Crocs for long enough can make any player reach for their wallet and buy some premium cosmetics.

Pokemon Go is finally bringing the Rookidee line from the Galar region into the game via the Steeled Resolve event.

#4183. Petit Planet Hands-On Preview – Creature Comforts

Petit Planet marks Hoyoverse’s maiden voyage into the life sim genre popularized by games like Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, and, most recently, Pokémon Pokopia. The creators of Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, and Zenless Zone Zero have crafted well-received, lucrative free-to-play gacha games across several disparate genres; Petit Planet, fittingly, sees it try to attract yet another world of players. It’s been a year since I first played Petit Planet’s initial alpha test, and I spent a couple of more hours exploring its cozy cosmos at the Hoyoverse Media Tour in Seoul, South Korea. Although what I played has not dramatically changed my opinion of the game – it remains a delightful, if familiar, good time – speaking to its lead designer who goes by the single name Murphy and lead artist Yunli Huang helped shed light on how Petit Planet will differentiate itself from contemporaries and its approach to multiplayer, storytelling, and monetization.

The game’s premise centers on a customizable protagonist who sets out to populate their own personal planet (which is about the size of King Kai’s world from Dragon Ball Z). Although you are ostensibly human, everyone else is a talking animal. Your mentor of sorts is a chillax sheepdog named Mobai, who enjoys wearing straw hats and dropping his catchphrase/life mantra “Mo worries” and “Mo Rush.” The business-minded Glenn the Squirrel is a shopkeeper and seems like a cuter, less aggressive Tom Nook. Yunghou is a shy fox who enjoys farming and has the slightest hint of a southern accent. These critters and many more inhabit your planet, which you’ll grow from an empty (but vibrant) rock into a bustling village filled with homes, businesses, crops, decor, and, of course, neighbors.

Story is rarely a hook for a genre that largely promotes creating your own fun through the emergent moments with your neighbors and friends in multiplayer. Still, after Pokémon Pokopia presented an unexpectedly wild and fascinating tale, I ask if players should bother getting invested in a grander narrative à la Genshin Impact. The short answer seems to be “not so much.”

“Unlike other Hoyoverse games, there is no such main plot,” Murphy explains in my group interview. “There will be a main story at the beginning, but the main purpose is just to guide the players, get more familiar with the setting and the world. But the whole narrative of this game will be more fragmented. For example, if you look at those descriptions of those items, there will be a lot of content and narrative behind it. If you look at the description of creatures, many of them are real creatures in real world, and you get to learn more knowledge of this creature by reading those descriptions. And also, we've developed a very comprehensive narrative for each of our neighbors, so that is also part of our, called like, main plot, main narrative, because we want to make this world more like more lively and a more livable world. So that is how we treat narrative in this game."

While players who enjoy a substantial story to propel them through a game may be disappointed, those looking to unwind with a laid-back experience should be pleased. Hoyoverse is designing Petit Planet to be a no-pressure experience to enjoy at your leisure, hence why it emphasizes it as a life sim more than a management sim. There are no complicated stats to manage; simple inputs make it easy to pick up and play; imperfection is encouraged, with Hoyoverse comparing the experience to doodling as a child: your creation may not be perfect, but you had fun bringing your imagination to life.

I spent the first hour of my roughly two-and-a-half-hour session starting from scratch to see if any notable changes were made to this introductory portion in the last year. If there are any differences, they’re imperceptible because I wen went through the same onboarding of learning how to catch bugs and fish, building your first home, inviting your first neighbor, and farming crops, all while growing a magical sapling that, after performing enough tasks, blooms into a full tree that brings new life and mechanics to your world as it grows. Performing special tasks for residents, from completing requests to simply interacting with them, grows their bond, which, when high enough, will entice them to move in. For veteran genre fans, it’s a familiar song and dance. What I did notice this time around is how refreshingly quick the onboarding is. You have all of these foundational mechanics within the first 45 to 50 minutes, which is a nice pace. It was a good refresher for some foundational mechanics I’d forgotten since I last played, but it created an appetite to dive deeper.

Thankfully, Hoyoverse provided a second build set many hours into the game to give an idea of how planets can evolve. This build was set during winter, one of Petit Planet’s revolving seasons that alter the environment and introduce themed cosmetics and decor for players and residents. Sporting winter gear, I ran around the snow-covered planet, which was densely populated with shops, homes, and neighbors. I was initially greeted by unfamiliar faces named Trixie and Kookoo, who provided weather forecasts and news reports reminiscent of Isabelle from Animal Crossing and Callie and Marie from Splatoon. My sparse quest log was tricky to tackle since they revolved around mechanics I had no context for, such as setting up Vignettes. These are essentially templates for unique scenes filled out by dropping the correct furniture pieces in their layout; in this case, I had to set up an outdoor movie on the beach.

I only spent roughly an hour with this late build, and my biggest takeaway was simply how dense and lovely the village looked. A lot of work went into crafting this build, which boasted a farm filled with different crops (with unlockable recipes to create dishes from them), crafting tables to build furniture from collectible blueprints, and several shops, including Glenn’s to purchase a revolving selection of decor items. None of what I saw surprised me, however. Petit Planet so far checks many of the boxes you’d expect and want from a life sim. My cursory tour of a later-game planet did little to reveal any big new ideas, but what I did experience seemed perfectly cromulent.

My biggest question regards multiplayer. As much as I enjoy Animal Crossing: New Horizons and Pokémon Pokopia as solo experiences, playing with friends feels like a mean joke because of the tedious number of hoops to jump through just to invite other players into your world. And even once your buddy arrives, interactions are disappointingly limited. When I ask if Petit Planet offers a comparatively frictionless multiplayer experience, Murphy vaguely assures smoother sailing. “The multiplayer experience is a very important part of our game because, just as the interaction with NPCs, the interaction with other players is also a form of building up emotional connection to this game, and we want to provide that kind of experience to our players.” More specifically, Murphy cites features such as dynamic server load adjustments based on player counts and the option to allow or ban visiting players from taking resources from your planet to prevent griefing.

As a free-to-play Hoyoverse game, monetization is a major talking point. In Petit Planet’s case, the team agrees that rolling for neighbors gacha-style would be strange and defeats the spirit of the genre. Instead, all monetization will revolve around cosmetics; players can unlock new furniture and themed decor sets, outfits, and other cosmetic accessories for their character. Unlocking a full themed set of decor earns currency points, and there are myriad reward meters to fill for performing mundane tasks like greeting residents or catching bugs. It remains to be seen if and how Petit Planet’s progression begins nudging players into opening their wallets, but Hoyoverse promises it will be an experience that deemphasizes grinding.

I also briefly checked out the recently announced Switch 2 version of Petit Planet. My impressions after about 15 minutes of playtime: it’s fine. It sometimes ran noticeably hitchier than the PC version I spent most of my time with, but it seems perfectly adequate so far and, hopefully, will be a smooth experience when it launches sometime next year.

Since life sims require more than a couple of hours to fully reveal their quality, it was tough to get a read on Petit Planet even with this new showing. The game looks beautiful thanks to Hoyoverse’s signature sharp and colorful visual style. It has a relaxing vibe, and feels mechanically decent for the most part. In short, it seems broadly fine and like a respectable take on the genre. I suspect its biggest appeal will be that it will receive what Animal Crossing: New Horizons lacked: years of constant, substantial support.

Hoyoverse is very good about keeping fans of its games well fed with regular updates for years on end, and I don’t expect it to stop now. The idea of a seemingly well-made spin on Animal Crossing that’s free to download and, unless it completely bombs, will almost certainly receive years of new content is enticing on paper. I imagine this is the reason Petit Planet is coming to Switch 2 next year, where it can lure in Animal Crossing and Pokopia players before other consoles. PC and mobile players, meanwhile, must only wait until December 4 when Petit Planet fully launches to see if it has the chops to stand alongside the coziest giants of the genre.

#4182. Genshin Impact fans on PS4 only have six weeks to find another platform as support winds down with one final update

Premium in-game purchases have now been disabled on PlayStation 4, as one of Genshin's four original launch platforms prepares to get dropped in early April.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

HoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's update.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

#4181. Pokemon's Beanie Bouncers Plushes Designed By Beanie Babies' Ty

Pokemon has just announced a new line of plushes that are quite a bit different from any of the soft toys it has ever released before. It has teamed up with Ty, the creators of Beanie Babies, to add some of its Pokemon and Poke Balls to the toy company’s Beanie Bouncers collection.

There are seven plushes in the Pokemon Beanie Bouncers collection to kick things off - three Pokemon and four Poke Balls. Jigglypuff, Voltorb, and Marill have been selected for Beanie Bouncer duty, while the Great Ball, Ultra Ball, Master Ball, and standard Poke Ball complete the lineup.

Only a week after its best set yet was released, details about three more Pokemon Lego sets have leaked.

There’s a reason why the entire first wave is made up of spherical Pokemon and objects. It’s because Beanie Bouncers are part plush, part bouncy ball. Unlike most plushes, which are designed to be cuddled and taken care of, the entire point of Beanie Bouncers is that they can bounce, so kids are actively encouraged to throw and kick them around.

Since they kind of have to be ball-shaped for that to work, the likes of Voltorb and Marill have been given the honor of debuting a new Pokemon plush type, with the usual suspects like Pikachu and Squirtle not really fitting the criteria required.

I’d bet my private cabin on the SS Anne that there will be a Pikachu Beanie Bouncer eventually. Especially if this first wave of plushes sells well.

There’s good news and bad news about these Pokemon Beanie Bouncers. The good news is they only cost 1,320 yen each, which is only a little more than $8. The bad news is that, although they’re being released today, they will exclusively be available in Japan.

That doesn’t mean those of us outside of Japan will never be able to buy them. Pokemon tends to release products in Japan first and then, if popular enough, ships them out to Pokemon Centers around the world. Since this is a collaboration with Ty that adds Pokemon-branded plushes to a range you can buy the world over, I’m more certain than ever that Pokemon Beanie Bouncers will be available everywhere, and probably pretty soon.

I’m, unfortunately, not so sure that will apply to the recently revealed Pokemon music box dioramas. The Pokemon Company revealed nine gorgeous diorama music boxes, one for each region, earlier this month. They’re exclusively available in Japan and feel like a more niche product that won’t be mass-produced, like Beanie Bouncers, and sold the world over.

You can now have a real Withered Wasteland of your own and fill it with Pokemon figures.

#4180. The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin may be your next anime gacha obsession, with a hint of Ghibli, and this latest trailer may be what sells you on it

There's another free-to-play action RPG very much on the horizon. Will this be the one to win you over?

It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another new entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

The gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet new characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

The game has a bit of an unusual release schedule. It’s set to arrive on PC, PS5, iOS, and Android. PC (Steam), and PS5 players will be able to jump in starting March 16, whereas the global mobile launch is scheduled for one week later, on March 23.

You can pre-register right now on the official website if you’re interested in earning a few rewards when the game launches. You can, of course, always wishlist the game on Steam and the PlayStation Store, too.

#4179. Grand Theft Auto VI Will Run At 30 FPS On All Consoles, But PS5 Pro Will Feature 'Improved Clarity' And Ray-Traced Shadows

Grand Theft Auto VI launches next week on Thursday, November 19, and you can preload the game on your PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S starting today, Rockstar Games has announced. The studio has also revealed what kind of visuals players can expect on their respective consoles, making clear that regardless of where you play, GTA VI targets 30 FPS gameplay.

"Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life – while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants," Rockstar writes in a blog post.

Rockstar Games also breaks down the different graphical settings available on PlayStation and Xbox consoles. On PS5 Pro, GTA VI will feature "improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro." On PS5 and PS5 Pro, the game will include "high-fidelity haptic feedback" fully integrated into DualSense controllers and adjustable via accessibility settings, improved spatial rendering so all in-game sounds take full advantage of Tempest 3D audio, and improved load times, "making Grand Theft Auto VI play best on PlayStation 5 consoles."

On Xbox consoles, Rockstar doesn't dive into performance; instead, it focuses on Xbox Cloud Gaming on Xbox Series X/S and Xbox One consoles, noting this feature will use Xbox Series S graphics settings.

GTA VI will also fully support Remote Play on PlayStation and Xbox.

GTA VI launches November 19 on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.

#4177. Marathon may actually have a shot as Server Slam hits it big on Steam

Marathon's latest public open weekend has kicked off, and it looks like enough people have showed up to play it.

Things are officially looking better for Marathon. The game’s Server Slam, essentially an open beta that’s freely available everywhere, has kicked off. This is the last chance for anyone curious about Bungie’s next big game to play it before it officially goes on sale next week.

Considering how unpopular the game has been throughout its development, and judging by the feedback from earlier closed beta tests, the turnout for the Server Slam is definitely encouraging.

The Marathon Server Slam has been online for a little over 12 hours on Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Only one of those platforms shares player numbers, of course, but it's enough to offer some visibility into how popular the test has been.

Immediately after servers went live, Marathon shot up the Steam most played charts. The game quickly achieved a peak of 143,621 concurrent players (via SteamDB), which is very respectable. Given that the Server Slam will be available for the entire weekend, there’s every chance the numbers will go up.

These figures are particularly encouraging when you look at Arc Raiders, the current top dog in the extraction shooter space, and the game that stole Marathon’s thunder last year when the two of them were being promoted by their publishers. Marathon, of course, got delayed out of 2025, which allowed Arc Raiders to launch first. It, of course, ended up proving that extraction shooters can be mainstream hits.

Like Marathon, Arc Raiders hosted its own server slam just a few days before its launch. That open test attracted 189,668 concurrent players at its peak, which is not that far off from Marathon’s so far.

Assuming positive word of mouth continues, more players are bound to jump in over the weekend and perhaps get Marathon to match or even exceed Arc Raiders’ record. At any rate, this is good news for beleaguered Bungie and points to what could be a big launch.

Marathon arrives March 5 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.

#4176. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 is about to launch a couple of major initiatives that may not exactly be what players have been looking for.

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

#4174. MTG's Nauctis: The Sunken Realm Makes Borderless Commanders A Premium Exclusive

The reveal of Nauctis: The Sunken Realm was supposed to be a cause for celebration. The full reveal of Magic: The Gathering’s first set of 2027, and it’s taking the TCG to a realm fans have been requesting for decades. Unfortunately, additional details about the set’s Commander decks have muted those celebrations somewhat.

The Sunken Realm will have four preconstructed Commander decks. Merfolk Reignment, Terrors of the Abyss, Blood in the Water, and Seal the Deal. A first look and the finer details of all four decks have been shared on the MTG website. However, it’s in those finer details that Magic players have spotted a problem.

There are changes coming to Magic in 2027, unpopular ones, and now those changes have been confirmed to begin with The Sunken Realm. A quick read of what exactly you’ll get with each of those four Commander decks reveals that standard decks will no longer include borderless versions of their face and featured commander cards.

We've got all the big news from the MagicCon Atlanta Preview Panel, which focuses on in-universe updates for 2027.

Scroll down a little further, and the situation goes from bad to worse. The borderless versions of those, now just standard foil, cards have been moved to the new set’s premium edition. Naturally, the premium edition of each deck is more expensive, $79.99 vs. $49.99, which means players and collectors will be forced to pay $30 more per deck for a perk that, until now, has been included in standard Commander decks.

But wait, there’s more. Not only will you now have to pay extra to get the borderless versions of The Sunken Realm’s face and featured commanders, but the foil used for the cards in the premium edition makes the pricier option even less desirable. The collector’s edition decks that premium edition versions seem to be replacing would use surge foil on their cards. The premium edition decks are now confirmed to use regular foil, yet they will still have the same MSRP.

The mere hint of these changes when a first look at these decks leaked ahead of time had Magic fans fearful. Now those changes have been confirmed, a lot of people are pretty upset. The top comment, for all the wrong reasons, on a Reddit thread getting a lot of attention on the r/mtgfinance subreddit simply reads “traditional foil”. Another accuses Wizards of the Coast of coming up with the laziest way possible to “crank up the prices”.

It’s a shame that Nauctis: The Sunken Realm’s reveal has been tainted by this since, as noted above, this is something traditional Magic fans have been waiting a long time for. Now the announcement of these unpopular changes has many less excited about diving into the new set next year, and instead questioning how they plan to approach it, and what they’re going to pre-order, if anything at all.

Please stop paying over the odds just because you can't wait a few months for a new Commander deck...

#4173. 10 Best Warhammer 40k Survivors in Warhammer Survivors

Shane is a Contributor for DualShockers writing guides and other materials. He has a degree in Game Design and Criticism.

While a lot of survivor-like games offer you plenty of characters to play, Warhammer Survivors, Warhammer's take on Vampire Survivors, takes it to a new level. With more than 40 characters to play as between both universes, you’re pretty spoiled for choice.

Just because there are a ton of characters to play, though, doesn’t mean they’re all particularly good. Some are a bit tougher to get the hang of than others, and some just have terrible stats.

Warhammer Survivors is a brutal spin-off of Vampire Survivors, pitting heroes from Warhammer 40,000 and Age of Sigmar against endless hordes of enemies while maintaining the addictive gameplay loop.

This list will give you the ten best survivors to play as in the Warhammer 40k universe, since heroes are not transferable between universes. Each one has their ups and downs, but for the most part, you’ll find one you'll be well suited to.

Of all the characters available in this wild roguelike game, Sister Superior Amalia Novena is undoubtedly the easiest to use. She comes with a weapon that keeps enemies at bay and will mostly wipe out low-level enemies in the early stages.

While she does have an upper limit, her increase in range for the first 30 levels can be a major game changer. She’s a great starter character to get a better feel for levels and for quickly completing objectives, without tricky mechanics to learn.

The thing about the lovely Canoness Aurora Veritas is that she’ll basically burn through waves of enemies like they’re nothing. Better weapons and status effects really help, especially when coming across the bosses with loads of health.

The only real downside is she also has an upper limit and doesn’t scale indefinitely. Her boosted range is helpful, but towards the end of runs, she just doesn’t have enough juice to really do much.

The Chaplain is a pretty average character when things get started, and their weapon isn’t all that reliable, but they can scale well into later game levels. Once you’ve unlocked plenty of weapons, you’ll pretty much always be getting a few followers with every level up.

The extra Range he gets, combined with the automatically boosted Veterancy, makes him a great candidate for almost any run. If you aren’t very far in your journey, though, he’s likely to be less than helpful.

Max is the definition of a run-and-gun FPS player, as he brings a Combat Shotgun and some serious ability strength with him. Gaining Strength with every level could see him scale incredibly quickly in the right build, making him stronger than most.

The fact that his ability has no upper limit means you can combine him with the Gauntlet passive to potentially double your damage. This will let him tear through hordes of enemies without any concern for his safety.

In terms of weapons, Sergeant Furan isn’t exactly rocking the best one there is, but he definitely makes up for it in other areas. If you stay healthy, you’ll be earning a lot more Skill, and if you find yourself in trouble, taking some damage can let you wipe out a horde.

With no upper limit to his scaling, Furan can get pretty powerful, especially with the right build of weapons and passives. A bit difficult to use when starting, but it does give you more control over the buff you have currently.

Warhammer Survivors takes the familiar Vampire Survivors formula and adds a fresh twist: players must forge a weapon to fight boss monsters.

There’s nothing better than running your enemies over and hearing their bones crush beneath your treads, which is exactly what Knight-Commander Pask is all about. With bonuses to Strength, Save, and Toughness, he’s a machine of war.

Thanks to that limitless scaling, after just ten levels you’ll be gaining a lot of Wounds back every second to keep you in the fight. He’s also a giant tank, and who doesn’t love driving a massive tank through their enemies?

Saint Celestine might seem like an angelic being, but when it comes to killing, she’s a total demon and can get some absurd builds going. She’s got extra speed and just gets better with every level you manage to acquire.

She even starts with a bonus to Chance and two extra Redeployments, all things that will make a run much easier from the outset. You won’t have an easy time getting the hang of her, but when you do, she’s truly a beast. That movement speed is just valuable.

One of the hardest characters to use thanks to her starting weapon, Aveline still tops the charts when it comes to dealing with enemies. Her weapon is tough to use, but when combined with the bonuses she gets to Range and Move, she can become very powerful very quickly.

She also comes with built-in Corruption and a free Banish, which definitely helps her in terms of gaining levels and getting what she wants. With a smart build, she can effectively wipe out a massive line of enemies in one go.

Daedalosus is a Technoarchaeologist, and he’s bringing the weirdness to the game in more ways than one. His permanent ability to always have four choices at level-up automatically makes him one of the best in the game, since that helps you to round out a build faster. He's amazingly versatile.

While not exactly the most busted in terms of raw power, he can be a great way to get coins quickly, which is only further improved by his 30% bonus to Tithe. He’ll need a good setup to get going, but once he’s going, he’s hard to stop in this strange roguelike.

As the very last survivor to unlock in the 40k setting, High Abbess Morvenn Vahl is an absolute powerhouse by every standard. With boosts to virtually every single stat in the game, and the extra utility of gaining bonus stats for each Adepta Sororitas follower, they’re made for battle.

In some of the best survivor-like games, the final survivor to unlock can feel underwhelming, but Morvenn lives up to their title all too well. Even though there's only a small number of Adepta Sororitas survivors in the game right now, they’re still almost unstoppable.

A review of Everything is Crab, a roguelite evolution-based game combining Survivor-like and Spore-like elements.

#4171. Our first look at Diablo 4's Warlock and the game's next season arrive in today's livestream - watch it here

Diablo 4's latest Developer Update is nearly upon us, and it's one plenty of the game's fans and players have been looking forward to.

Diablo 4’s next, long-awaited Developer Update finally airs today. This meaty livestream was first announced nearly a month ago, when Blizzard initially revealed that the game’s next class is the Warlock.

The Warlock’s initial unveiling, however, was incredibly brief, showing no gameplay. It also didn't explain how the class is going to fit within the existing roster. This all changes today.

Blizzard is bringing back its Developer Update livestream programme, which is the more structured, information-dense series of developer showcases. The focus of this one, of course, is going to mainly be on the Warlock class.

The Warlock is one of two classes coming to Diablo 4 with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion. The first, the Paladin, is already available in the game for anyone who pre-orders the expansion. The Warlock will instead arrive alongside the expansion on April 28.

The Developer Update will also include a first look at the game’s next season (Season 12), currently set for March 10. This mini season will only last until the expansion’s release, so it’s going to be interesting to see what it brings to the game.

You’ll be able to watch the showcase live at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT on Diablo 4’s official YouTube, Twitch, and Twitter channels. We’ve embedded the YouTube and Twitch players below for your convenience.

Among the topics the Developer Update will cover are the Killstreaks system, as well as Bloodstained items. As always, you can also expect a Q&A segment at the end of the show, and I imagine there’s going to be a few about the Warlock.

#4170. House House Discloses AI Use For 'Under 0.1%' Of Big Walk's Code Following IGF Voting Controversy

Big Walk developer House House has found itself at the center of a controversy over the upcoming Independent Games Festival on March 3, 2027, after a group of its jurors said they would not vote for any game that has used generative AI in any capacity. The jurors' statement does not name House House or Big Walk, but the studio eventually updated its FAQ to explain how it used generative AI for coding after IGF discussions. After vaguely posting on social media, those associated with IGF made clear that a sticking point in the voting process was Big Walk.

Former games journalist and game developer Austin Walker posted the IGF jurors' statement on Bluesky, explaining that voting has been difficult this year due to the "significant increase in the number of submitted games developed with generative AI tools."

"This has set off some fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools, and at this point there is no universal consensus on what (if anything) is to be done," the statement reads. "The IGF has affirmed that we may cast our votes according to our own tastes and values. But we, as a contingent of IGF jurors, feel that this trend and the games embracing it deserve stronger pushback than a vote in silence."

The statement continues, explaining that not all jurors are on board with the blanket statement, citing reasons including "their ability to safely sign without professional blowback." It continues, "Above all: Our goal is to state solidarity with those who despair over the future of their art, their craft, and their industry – including those who have experimented with these tools, but who now believe they are not in our best interest."

The statement continues with the jurors' beliefs regarding gen-AI, including its negative effects, that any gen-AI used in any process of game development is not okay, noting specifically that "AI-generated code is not an exception to these harms," and more.

"For those reasons, this year we are declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity," the statement says. "We urge the IGF to adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future years that disallows games containing any AI-generated work." The statement then includes the names of the IGF jurors who signed it.

Big Walk isn't specifically mentioned within that statement. However, Kyle LeClair, a four-time IGF judge and a juror for the upcoming IGF, tells Aftermath that "it got to the point where the most-discussed game this year almost entirely involved its AI usage, overshadowing pretty much everything else." LeClair says it felt like a boiling point, adding, "Anyhow, strong props to the jurors for taking this stance and putting out this letter as well, even if some people believe that using AI for coding purposes is a more gray area, we're at a point where the amount of AI slop clogging up the indie game scene means having to take hard stances such as this in order to discourage such an amount of recklessness."

Again, no mention of Big Walk. However, game developer Bruno Diaz took to BlueSky to confirm the speculation: that most-discussed game was Big Walk. "Okay, because the cat is out of the f---ing bag, I might as well combat misinformation a bit: 1. The reason IGF judges are aware of the LLM use in the development of Big Walk is through a disclosure shared by House House. 2. This disclosure was required by IGF rules. 3. While some have characterized the LLM usage as just fixing one individual blocking bug, this is a bit inaccurate; the description given by House House mentioned there being several instances, though they did also say it was mostly 'consultative' use and not code gen or agents."

Diaz notes that they believe that distinction is without a difference, adding that "to my knowledge, it is not the case that Big Walk is non-compliant with the former [Steam's AI disclosure requirements]."

"Yes, there was a large discussion about this in internal IGF forums," Diaz said. "Yes, a lot of people said things that I personally think were disingenuous, extremely disappointing, or just (frankly) dumb. No, I have no intention of talking about it in further detail or exposing anyone. [...] Ultimately, it is extremely difficult for a group of over 100 people to keep a secret so I expected this to come out eventually. Shrug emoji. If you think something is reputationally damaging, consider not doing it."

With discussion surrounding Big Walk happening during the IGF discussions, House House updated its FAQ to address, "Was AI used to make Big Walk?" Here's what the FAQ reads, in full:

"In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs. In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.

The primary use case for House House’s use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code. If you’re technically-minded, and curious, here’s an example. We needed to cull shadow casters by distance from the camera, but Unity URP only allows culling shadow casters by distance in camera forwards, so shadow casters behind the player were being rendered at an infinite distance. This made our game run 50% slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset. We researched the problem extensively, and we looked at the URP code ourselves, but we couldn’t find a way. Then, we were able to speak directly to an engineer at Unity, who asked around and ultimately concluded that what we wanted wasn’t possible. Finally, we posed the question to an LLM chatbot. After a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked. This fix represented about 10 lines of code inside URP.

We originally wrote a version of the above disclosure as it was a suggested part of our IGF submission. We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest.

This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as “inevitable”. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.

Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

As you can see, House House did not disclose its use of AI-generated code because "Steam as a platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage." It says it is posting the disclosure now as "it has become a matter of public interest."

House House recently made headlines for choosing not to put Big Walk on Xbox in accordance with the Palestinian-led BDS boycott against Microsoft Games. Earlier this year, it gained widespread critical acclaim for its unique emphasis on cooperative puzzle-solving – you can read more about that in Game Informer's Big Walk review.

#4169. Diablo 4's next season is short, but it lets you become The Butcher, and it has Doom: The Dark Ages skins you probably can't afford

Blizzard has unveiled the next Diablo 4 season, which kicks off next week to hold us over until the launch of the game's big expansion in April.

The big Diablo 4 Developer Update has indeed delivered the goods. One of the livestream’s big topics was, of course, the game’s upcoming mini-season, which is set to kick off next week and run until the launch of Lord of Hatred, the game’s anticipated next expansion.

You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.

Season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion. Many of the season’s biggest additions were available to preview in the 2.6.0 Public Test Realm.

Patch 2.6.0, as you might have guessed, is the one that will kick off the slaughter next week. The headline feature here is ability to become The Butcher, the iconic in-game boss who randomly invades players’ games.

When you play as The Butcher, you’ll be rewarded the more kills you get in quick succession. Your skills hotbar will transform to become something more fitting of The Butcher, making them more brutal. You’ll also earn a seasonal currency as you play.

Starting the seasonal questline is how you can begin to assume The Butcher’s form. A Taste of Power can be initiated from Gea Kul. Transforming into The Butcher can be done in a few ways. As you play, you’ll earn Meaty Offerings, which can later be spent on Shrines of Slaughter in the new Helltide. Once activated, the shrine will draw more enemies towards you.

If you never venture into PvP zones in Diablo 4, this season may change your mind. The standard PvP combat that could only be found in Fields of Hatred has been replaced with a Ceremony of Slaughter, a new event that rewards you for killing enemies quickly. See it through and The Butcher’s Idol will spawn, allowing you to transform into it.

Elsewhere in the world, you’ll also be able to attain the same power at Slaughterhouses, a new activity type available this season. Inside, you immediately become The Butcher for the entirety of the run.

The Butcher’s arrival also ties into two of the other Season of Slaughter’s more interesting additions. First, the Killstreak system finally arrives in Diablo 4, rewarding you for being as efficient as possible in carving your way through enemies.

Anyone who played Diablo 3 should be familiar with how it works. It kicks off the moment you get a kill, and has a visible timer where you’ll need continue performing the same action to up your streak. The more kills you get, the more often your timer will refresh.

There are five tiers to climb through: Killstreak, Carnage, Devastation, Bloodbath, and Massacre. You’re awarded for the tier you manage to reach before the timer runs out. You’ll earn XP and seasonal rep each time a Killstreak is achieved.

The other Butcher-themed addition is Bloodied Items, which is a new item quality available throughout this season. They play into the Killstreak system to grant you even more power. Bloodied Items come with unique affixes that scale off your Killstreak tier. You’ll see many familiar items in that pool, as any item in the game has a chance to drop as Bloodied. Bloodied Items can also be acquired by earning Fresh Meat.

Even if none of that sounds exciting, you’re probably going to redownload the game for The Paladin free trial, which kicks off alongside the new season on March 11. The trial is only available until March 18, and it lets you try out the Paladin class.

The trial is available across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. You’ll be able to take the new class for a spin, but your progress will be capped at level 25. The Paladin can be permanently unlocked by buying the Lord of Hatred expansion, as it’s one of two classes the expansion is introducing.

The good news is that any progress you make in the free trial will carry over to the full game if/when you buy the expansion.

Season of Slaughter also kicks off a Doom: The Dark Ages collaboration event. As we’ve come to expect, there’s a very limited free component to the collaboration, in the form of the Doom Reliquary. This is essentially a mini-battle pass that includes the Shield Saw skin, Slayer’s Flair, the head of the Cyberdemon as a back trophy and various other smaller bits.

The more impressive items - such as character skins, will instead be available to purchase for real money. The list includes the Doom Slayer armor, Mecha Dragon Serrat skin for your cat mount, and a Cacodemon pet.

Though the armor skin is cross-class compatible, judging by how much previous collaboration items have cost in Diablo 4, most of us probably won’t be spending that kind of money to get it.

#4168. Pikmin 4 Is Still Great, But Dandori Academy Is Underwhelming

Pikmin 4 was released for the original Switch in 2023, and it ranks among my favorite games on the platform; I happily award it the honor of being the best Pikmin game. It looks and plays great, and Oatchi the dog makes the sometimes annoying process of managing a collection of little plant creatures willing to do your bidding much smoother.

The over-titled Pikmin 4 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy releases November 12, and much like other comparable Nintendo games that have been ported and improved for Switch 2 (like Kirby and Mario Party), the base game is as good as it was initially and looks even better. If you skipped Pikmin 4 on Switch for whatever reason (probably because it was day one of the Barbenheimer epidemic), I encourage you to play it now. You have about a week to beat it before… something else comes out. Who’s to say.

The “big” addition here for the Switch 2 version of the game, alongside improved performance and visuals and the ability to give Oatchi verbal commands, is Dandori Academy. The Academy is an expanded time trial mode that awards medals for practicing specific levels, which you can then play and upload your high scores on specific days. For example, I can play the Advanced B level, Rockaway Cellars, as much as I want, but it only really counts if I play it on November 12. And you only get one try (though you can unlock retry tickets).

In theory, I like the unique approach to high-score battling, and the limited timeframe adds fun intensity, but this isn't what I am looking for from Pikmin. I recognize and acknowledge the design decision to place timers on your interactions in Pikmin, but it’s never been my favorite part. I like building my adorable little army and exploring, discovering, and retrieving as many unexpected items as possible. But I mostly get annoyed at the ticking clock, especially when I am watching my crew meander toward my spaceship holding a Game Boy Advance SP (or whatever they manage to find on the never-acknowledged, but potentially post-apocalyptic Earth you are exploring).

I also like having a list of missions to complete, and in Dandori Academy, there isn’t much acknowledgment of your success in practice. You can earn a platinum medal while practicing Rockaway Cellar, but it’s mainly to let you know that this is what you could earn when you play on the right day.

The main takeaway is that Pikmin 4 is still excellent, and I was grateful to transfer my save file from the Switch version (and I was tempted to start a new game + save), but Dandori Academy is not a strong incentive to return if you already played the game. It is a nice bonus and an interesting concept that reimagines the familiar time trial mode featured in plenty of video games, but the original campaign is still the main attraction.

#4167. Grammy Nominees For Best Video Game Soundtrack Announced

The nominees for this year's Grammy Awards have been announced, a ceremony that has handed out an award for best video game soundtrack since 2023. Five games have made the shortlist this year, with some of the biggest titles from the past 12 months making the shortlist for their respective scores.

The five games with OSTs vying for a Grammy award this year are 007: First Light, Marvel's Wolverine, Ghost of Yotei, Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora - From the Ashes, and Star Wars: Zero Company. The winner of the award won't be revealed until Sunday, February 7, 2027, when the annual Grammys ceremony takes place.

As is often the case when it comes to awards eligibility, it might seem a little odd to see a game like Ghost of Yotei on the list since it was released over a year ago. In fact, it will have been available for close to 18 months by the time the Grammys take place in February of next year.

The 2027 Grammys eligibility period incorporates anything that was released between August 31, 2025, and August 28, 2026. Since Yotei was released in October 2025, it qualifies for a nomination. The same applies to Avatar's From The Ashes DLC, which was released in December 2025. It's actually odd that Wolverine has made the cut since that wasn't released until September 15, 2026, after this year's eligibility window had technically closed.

It's nominated nonetheless, which means four out of five of this year's Grammys video game OST nominees are from licensed games. In the five years that this award has existed, 14 out of 25 of the nominees have been licensed games, but only one licensed game has ever won it. That honor went to Star Wars Jedi: Survivor in 2024.

This will also be the third year in a row that Frontiers of Pandora has been nominated. Its base game was nominated in 2025, then its first DLC last year, and now its From The Ashes expansion.

Aside from Jedi: Survivor in 2024, other previous winners of the Grammy Award for best video game soundtrack include Sword of the Sea and Assassin's Creed Valhalla's Dawn of Ragnarok expansion. Those responsible for voting received heavy criticism last year after Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's soundtrack wasn't even nominated.

Many games have been nominated for tons of awards at The Game Awards over the years, but which series brought home the most?

#4166. Diablo 4’s Warlock looks like an unhinged Necromancer with Sorcerer energy in first look at gameplay

Diablo 4's practitioner of forbidden arts, The Warlock, has been officially unveiled as the second class coming with Lord of Hatred.

Thanks to a meaty, well-produced Diablo 4 Developer Update, we got to have our promised first look at gameplay of the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The showcase offered a deep look at the Warlock’s core archetypes, its gameplay and skills loop, and where the class sits within the game’s existing roster of diverse classes.

Since the initial reveal of Lord of Hatred, The Warlock has remained the mysterious second class. Anyone who pre-purchased the expansion was able to get immediate access to The Paladin, the other class arriving with the expansion. It wasn’t until February that Blizzard officially revealed the class to the world, but we had to wait until this most recent Developer Update to actually see it in action.

The Warlock’s pragmatism exists as the counterpart to The Paladin's purity, in that Warlocks don’t shy away from harnessing the powers of Hell to eliminate their enemies. The class can conjure up demons to do their bidding, and utilise attacks previously only available to legions of Hell.

The Warlock is a hybrid pet and caster class. Their gameplay revolves around summoning demons, and undermining enemies with shadow arts. They rely on two resources: Wrath, and Dominance. Casting Skills consumes Wrath, whereas Dominance is what allows the Warlock to summon and exploit demons.

The Warlock has four archetypes players can spec into. Legions are traditional summoners who rely on overwhelming numbers to crush enemies. Vanguards are closer to Sorcerers, capable of dealing damage head-on. Masterminds utilise shadowcraft to slowly drain their enemies. Finally, Ritualists are summoners of the most terrifying Hell demons.

The Warlock is able to do this by fusing Soul Shards into their bodies. Going down any of the four paths becomes available after reaching level 30, which is when the class mechanic is unlocked. Each Soul Shard is tied to a certain demon, and its through that power that the Warlock is able to call upon them in combat. Your choice does, of course, affect your abilities going forward.

Warlocks arrive alongside new Uniques that cater to their specific playstyles, which is similar to what we’ve previously seen with The Paladin, and The Spiritborn before that.

Lord of Hatred arrives April 28. While we wait, Diablo 4’s next season is kicking off next week to deliver a bit of mindless fun to hold us over until the big day.

Queen's Domain has got me royally hooked. After a somewhat confusing and frustrating start, I'm now deep into the game in all but actual progression, and its classic PC stylings and game design are just ticking so many boxes I'd forgotten I had.

It's still frustrating, but lord help me am I going to push on through this weekend.

So I played Alone in the Dark last weekend, as promised. It's not great. However, Queen's Domain is great, so I definitely plan to put a bit more time into it over the next few days or so.

Despite the very minor upgrades, I'm also keen to dive into Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy. The visuals have definitely received a nice bump in quality, so it'll be nice to experience the campaign in glorious 4K.

I have other games that I want to squeeze in before 2026 is up, but I simply haven't been able to pry myself away from Ocarina of Time yet. I was so unsure about it from the initial reveal, but goodness me, I love this remake so much.

Despite my best efforts to stretch it out for as long as possible, I only have a few dungeons to go at this point. I'm going to be a wreck at the finale.

The kids and I are heading up Death Mountain this weekend, although by the time you read this we’ve probably already done in Dodongo and are beansing it to Zora’s Domain.

Unfortunately, playing through Ocarina my spawn means that I can’t continue once they’ve gone to bed. And yet despite having dozens of 2026's finest to be getting on with (finished Mixtape this week, great stuff), I’m stuck in a very enjoyable COD funk, with all sorts of numbers in multiplayer. Have a good one, folks.

Those are our plans, but what about yours? Let us know what you'll be slapping in your Switch (2) in the poll below.

Nintendo Life’s resident horror fanatic, when he’s not knee-deep in Resident Evil and Silent Hill lore, Ollie likes to dive into a good horror book while nursing a lovely cup of tea. He also enjoys long walks and listens to everything from TOOL to Chuck Berry.

Well, after last week’s rather unfortunate timing of my daughter falling ill on the very day Ocarina of Time launched, I’m delighted to report she’s made a full recovery and has officially started nursery! A big week of milestones in our household, both in Hyrule and the real world.

As for Link, things have escalated rather dramatically. I met a lovely sage who kindly aged me seven years, returned to Castle Town to find the neighbourhood had gone downhill somewhat, and encountered a deeply unsettling graveyard child with a worrying obsession with skull masks.

Since then, I’ve managed to keep pace with the restless soul of Dampé, who rewarded my efforts with a shiny new Hookshot, and I’m now knee deep in the Forest Temple. I’ve also accidentally consumed an alarming number of poes. Don’t ask.

I’m hoping to keep up a steady pace of a temple or two a week from here, all while enjoying the build-up to a very special Christmas as my beautiful daughter approaches her first birthday. Watching her discover the world while I rediscover Hyrule feels rather fitting, really.

Tonight I'm not seeing my friends so I'll just continue with my schedule:

Ultros: starting my 3rd time-loop, really curious how this will go and hoping I'm not heading to a dead-end XD

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort: been playing Island Crown at Tennis and Bowling, and unlocking all sorts of queer items 🤭. Ah, that good old Wii Sports! 😍

Tetris Effect: Connected: participating in the weekend ritual, as usual ...

And SMB Wonder, RP Groove and MK World will be the three multiplayer contenders...

Have fun, happy gaming, and make the most of your weekend! ✌🏻🧡🎮

Sonic Generations: The 3DS version, specifically. It's absolutely terrible. I've played a lot of bad Sonic games, but this is something else. I'm currently at the final boss and I feel like I've sunk into the centre of the Triceratops poop in Jurassic Park. The controls just don't make sense; sometimes they behave exactly as they should, while sometimes they literally do the exact opposite of what I've pressed. I don't know if I'll finish this game, but I do know that if I don't finish it then I won't lose sleep over it.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026): I rolled credits on this last night and… wow. No game is truly perfect but, as a remake, this is perfect. Faithful yet tweaked where you'd want it to be, and utterly gorgeous on top. It feels weird to say that a 2026 remake of a 1998 game is my game of the year so far and worth buying a Switch 2 for, but Ocarina of Time is my game of the year so far and worth buying a Switch 2 for.

Professor Layton and the Curious Village: I'm still chipping away at this; a few puzzles here, a few puzzles there. Will I ever finish it? Who knows? Does it still make me feel like a dullard incredibly frequently? Yes.

Super Mario 3D Land and New Super Mario Bros. 2: There are still secret exits and star coins to find, and I will find them all!

Additionally, even though I've played through Ocarina of Time, Skyward Sword HD and Tears of the Kingdom over the past few months, I'm already hankering for more Zelda. I'm torn between A Link Between Worlds, or either of Oracle of Ages/Oracle of Seasons. I've not played any of them before. Or maybe I do yet another playthrough of The Minish Cap? 👀

I’ve also accidentally consumed an alarming number of poes. Don’t ask.

This weekend I will be working towards the endgame of Final Fantasy Resonance. Just reached the big reveal of Umbra's identity which I guessed ages ago but despite some predictability in the narrative I still think the writing is really strong and I'm connecting with the characters in a way I have with the best Final Fantasy games prior.

Will also put more time into the excellent Queen's Domain. The game is really starting to open up now that I have evolved a weapon and bested the first boss netting the big game changer traversal reward for that accomplishment. Still have to play with the utmost caution but I love the game so far.

Finally more Street Fighter 6 and Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered with the kids. At the request of my son we'll also put more time into Super Smash Bros. Ultimate. I hadn't played in years so he stomped me the first few rounds but my muscle memory kicked in and I sent him packing to Kingdom Hearts with Sora.

More OOT of course 👍 Still only in the early game as Ive had a lot on, in and out of work. Equally, I dont want to rush the experience as every moment I am thoroughly enjoying.

Im in the market for another CRT so might do some hunting for one to add to my retro setup.

Rest of the weekend, probably some Burnout Takedown. 170+ events in the game and Im trying to get gold in each.

Well, this was quite a week in terms of reducing and expanding the backlogs. I'm finally through with Nonograms Prophecy...at least with what I could access of it because the last two Big Picture slots still say "in progress" while solving everything else in the mode still left the counter at 0/10 (a remarkable counter in itself because there are 9 big pictures without the unplayable tutorial as is, 11 with the missing stuff and 12 if you do count the tutorial). Might be DLC stuff but the page shows no signs of the latter, and honestly? After 40 hours, I think I'm good.😄

I've also finally wrapped up Wolfenstein: The New Order and dipped my toes into The Old Blood, but The New Colossus is more of a priority now. Where to install it, though? Ah, that's a whole other story. The 512 Gb Express SanDisk gambled with at a regional online marketplace (after the only Minsk retailer previously stocking it messaged me back about not getting any more stuff shipped in) arrived last Sunday night, getting properly recognized by the console right on pickup... then repeatedly heating up and autoejected in the laptop beyond 4 Gb of data (from the backups to avoid redownloading). I had done enough reading about online marketplace fakes and their proverbial real capacity that my immediate reactions defy sharing here in public, but tested the thing in Switch 2 again... and it does work there?🤔 Everything from the previously installed stuff to the newly added FFXIV trial and the retrieved Gamecube app downloaded and proceeded to run without a hitch. Knocking on wood here, but the bullet may have been ultimately dodged.

Anyhoo, the Gen 10 storage expansion with roughly 80 Gb left of it even urged me to pull the trigger on the juicy FFVIIR discounts after all, although both games are 10 Gb bigger, unlikely to get completed before Xenoblade 3's bloa- er, upgraded filesize arrives (not to mention next year's Genesis) and still probably best benched at least until I finish Crisis Core. What did get installed from the spoils of the same eShop top-up is Drop Duchy and Souldiers, if at the expense of Vampire Hunters on OLED. What? New Colossus? Right - so the aforementioned 256 Gb card became predictably vacant and I'm still too unenthused about last gen's period of juggling multiple cards per console (what with repeatedly powering on and off in the process) to use it properly, so I really just went and boosted Mariko's storage towards many a previously shelved playthrough instead. New Colossus and Biomutant, Haven and Snake Pass, Layers of Fear 2 and Mad Rat Dead, Immortals and Starlink, Amalur and Dragon's Dogma, Outer Worlds and Pillars of Eternity, Astral Chain and Nocturne, Nelke and WoFF, Diablo 2 and Rebel Galaxy Outlaw, Red Dead Redemption and Devil Ma- never mind, the last one promptly got kicked back out to accommodate New Colossus last night. No, no room left to immediately reinstall Vampire Hunters but you can't win them all.

Needless to say, the weekend's hybrid appetites are encompassing the whole list above alongside the OLED's (Ball x Pit, Drop Duchy, KH1, Eternia, Yumia, Potion Permit, DerQ, and AC2) and NS2's (Motorfest, RE4, FFXIV, Cyberpunk, Tales of Arise, XC2 and Factorio) respective troves. Barely even making plans for the handhelds as a result, although some Flotsam, Xenosaga, Gravity Rush and Chase Begins may still show up on the menu. And that's enough of my first world pseudoblog.😅

That's my weekend sorted right there, but after that? ...heck, I don't know what comes next! Maybe a Layton replay to prep for New World of Steam? Me and my 5 year old weean have been playing Pikmin 4 this past month.

Now the upgrade is here he’s been absolutely delighted to order Oachi about and it’s actually helping pronunciation of his second language cos Oachi’s a finicky bugger at times.

In fact, much like my son, Oachi seems to have very selective hearing and doesn’t take well to commands but picks up even the faintest, mumbled utterance of praise. I’ll say ‘good job’ as my son herds his Pikmin away from a boss attack only for Oachi to stop in his tracks as his senseless spaceman jockey pats him on the head as masses of Pikmin fall to a follow up attack. Then my son gets upset.

The game looks completely beautiful since the upgrade and the people refusing to buy it at 30fps are missing Nintendo at their artistic and creative zenith. Stunning game in every sense - I walked over a small patch of tin foil this afternoon and of course Nintendo recorded specific footsteps for it.

Seeing my son recall character names better than me and watching him judder as something creepy crawly pops into view has been priceless. Cherished time.

#4164. Marvel Cosmic Invasion's Doctor Doom-Themed DLC Gives It The Post-Game Tail It Was Missing

Marvel Cosmic Invasion was a bit of a dream game for me; I loved the X-Men arcade game in the '90s, so when Tribute Games released the excellent Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge in 2022, I immediately hoped they'd revitalize other licensed brawler franchises released by Konami in the late '80s and early '90s. While we still haven't heard any word of a new brawler starring The Simpsons, Tribute did follow up its Turtle triumph with Marvel Cosmic Invasion, another throwback side-scrolling beat 'em up, this time starring Marvel's mightiest.

I played through Marvel Cosmic Invasion multiple times and had a blast, but I moved on quickly, as I didn't feel the need to collect different palette-swaps of the many heroes on offer. Even after Cyclops and The Thing joined the roster as DLC in May, I still saw Cosmic Invasion as a game in the rearview. That changes this week, as The Siege of Castle Doom not only adds two additional playable characters (Invisible Woman and Doctor Doom), but also a mode that has the potential to bring me back for more runs for the foreseeable future.

Seeing that Annihilus is threatening the universe, Doom decides to take matters into his own hands. Unfortunately, much in the way that it seems that he may try to fix the multiversal incursions in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, Victor Von Doom's solution in Marvel Cosmic Invasion – the Cosmic Inductor – would lead to untold death and destruction. In The Siege of Castle Doom, you select your team and fight your way through various floors of the stronghold belonging to the man who is perhaps Marvel's greatest villain. Your goal is to fight through the winding, randomized hallways of Castle Doomstadt, charging Reed Richards' Stabilizer and tactically bolstering your team along the way, before Doctor Doom can enact his plan.

As for the new playable characters, Doctor Doom is less agile, but his attacks pack a whallop, while Invisible Woman's force fields and speed make her the more versatile pick. I don't know that I see either of them replacing my mains from the base game, but I had fun experimenting with them throughout this mode. Regardless of which character you choose from the expanding roster, you still must traverse Castle Doomstadt before Doom achieves his objective.

Fighting through waves of enemies across differently themed and booby-trapped rooms, you encounter all manner of foes from the base game, as well as new minion types from Doom. When you defeat enemies, they drop batteries that charge your Stabilizer, letting you even the odds and stop Doom. Conversely, each time an enemy hits your character, it charges Doom's Cosmic Inductor, inching him closer to victory and making his minions faster and stronger in the process. As you might expect, the rooms get harder the deeper you go, and while each player starts with two characters to swap between, if a character completely depletes their health, they're gone for good, making it even tougher. As such, you need to keep your eyes on each character's health and swap them out when it makes sense.

As you complete each room, you can choose which path to take to augment your characters with new special abilities. True to the roguelite structure, as you complete rooms, you can also buff your characters' stats within the run. Certain rooms offer extra batteries to help your Stabilizer charge, while others offer new and upgraded equipment. There's also one that promises random events that can easily alter the trajectory of your run for better or worse. Though I often enjoyed boosting attack stats to make enemies less like damage sponges, I had to balance that against buffing their health to keep them alive and charging the Stabilizer to have a fighting chance.

Beyond the in-run upgrades and modifiers, you can also amp up the action run-over-run through upgrades in Reed's Lab, which add to the pool of modifiers you can select from at the start of each run. The expansion also adds new palettes for existing heroes, plus new music by composer Tee Lopes. While I've only done a few runs of The Siege of Castle Doom (each taking between 45 and 90 minutes, depending on how successful you are), I feel a revitalized sense of excitement for Marvel Cosmic Invasion. Tribute claims completionists can spend upwards of 15 hours in this new mode, which has me champing at the bit to dive back into what will likely be my primary way of interacting with Marvel Cosmic Invasion going forward.

Marvel Cosmic Invasion – The Siege of Castle Doom is available today on all platforms, and it is a strong addition to an already great game. You can read our review of the base version of Marvel Cosmic Invasion here.
